item.title: The open door is a lottery
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Why the habits that made a small team fast start making it slow around 50
item.category: Growing faster than it's getting clearer
item.content:encoded:
At ten people, you don’t have to tell anyone anything. They were in the room.

At ten, there are 45 possible one-to-one conversations in the company. You’re part of most of them. A decision gets made on Tuesday, and by Wednesday lunch everyone knows. Nobody announced it. The building is just small enough that news travels on its own.

At fifty, there are 1,225.

Nobody can hold 1,225 relationships. Not you, not your best operator, not the person at the front desk who seems to know everything. So information stops moving because people are around, and starts moving by rumor, by proximity, and by whoever happened to be in the kitchen. Fred Brooks made this point about software teams in 1975. When you add people, the communication load doesn’t grow in a straight line. It grows in a curve. The arithmetic hasn’t changed since.

Why the number keeps coming up

I’m wary of magic numbers. (Confession: I’m writing another book, Seven: the biography of a number. See As You Like It. IYKYK.) Sorry, back. Nothing happens at exactly 50 that didn’t happen at 47. But several unrelated lines of evidence land in the same neighborhood, and when that happens I pay attention.

Robin Dunbar, the Oxford anthropologist who first proposed 150 as the limit on stable relationships, also found that human relationships cluster in layers of roughly 5, 15, 50 and 150. Each layer is about three times the size of the one before, and closeness drops at every step. The 50 layer is people you know but don’t see often. Grow past it, and the founder has quietly moved most of the company into the outer ring. People still say hello to you. They no longer know what you’re thinking.

The law notices too. In the US, family leave, the Affordable Care Act’s employer mandate and, for federal contractors, a written affirmative action plan for workers with disabilities all start at 50. In France, so many labor rules kick in at 50 that economists Luis Garicano, Claire Lelarge, and John Van Reenen found more than twice as many firms with 49 employees as with 50: companies choosing not to grow rather than cross the line.

So the claim isn’t “exactly 50.” It’s around 50. Somewhere past 40, the way you’ve been running things starts costing more than it gives.

What breaks first

Two habits break first, and they break together.

The first is the open door. Every founder is proud of it: anyone can walk in, any time. At ten people, that’s a gift. At fifty, it’s a lottery. The people who use it are already close, sit nearby, or feel confident enough to knock. Everyone else gets their information secondhand.

The second is word-of-mouth updates. At ten, telling three people is telling everyone. At fifty, telling three people starts a rumor, and by the time it reaches the far end of the building, someone has edited it at every stop.

The handbook answer is the familiar one: write it down, hold a regular all-hands, publish a weekly update, open a channel. Do all of that. None of it is wrong. The founder-mode answer is to keep the door open and walk the floor more. That isn’t wrong either.

Both miss that the open door was never a communication system. It was you. You were the hub, and the company ran on how close people sat to you. A newsletter doesn’t change that. If you keep making real decisions in the doorway and announcing them later, the all-hands becomes the place where people learn what the insiders knew last week.

I call this keeping the license. The all-hands has the title: it’s officially where decisions get shared. You’ve kept the license: the real decision still happens wherever you happen to be standing. Everyone can tell. You’ll see this pattern again every day this week.

Closing the door isn’t the fix either. I once had a new boss who rarely left her office and kept her door shut on principle. She didn’t last.

The shift is in you, not the org chart

Around 50, the leader’s job changes from being available to being deliberate. Being available means: come and find me. Being deliberate means: I’ll tell you first, myself, and then I’ll tell you again.

Founders hate that second telling. It feels redundant. You said it in the leadership meeting and mentioned it in Slack, so surely people know. They don’t. By the time you’re sick of saying something, the far end of the company is just hearing it for the first time, usually from someone who heard it from someone else.

Heads of school and nonprofit directors hit the same wall: the building got bigger, but the habit didn’t change.

The move this week

Each issue this week ends with one page of a five-page audit. Keep the pages together. Friday’s page uses the other four.

Page one. Take the last significant decision you made: a hire, a change in priorities, a budget call, anything people would care about.

Make two lists.

  1. Who heard about it directly from you, before they heard it anywhere else?

  2. Who heard about it secondhand, or found out because they noticed?

Be honest about the second list. If you’re not sure how someone found out, put them on it.

Then look at what separates the two lists. I’d bet it isn’t seniority or need-to-know. It’s distance: who sits near you, who you already talk to, who knocked.

That’s your open door, measured. Most leaders find the first list is shorter than they expected, and that the people on the second list are the ones who most needed to hear it from them. Keep both lists. That’s page one.

Tomorrow: what happens when everything still goes through you.

When growth outruns how you lead, my free diagnostic calls that pattern the Growth Gap. It takes two minutes, and your readout appears on screen with no email wall.

My book CLUTCH: How Leaders Build Systems That Run Without Them is the long version of this week’s argument: leadership as a system you design, not a set of habits you hope will scale. It’s a paperback, built to be worked in with a pencil.

item.title: It's his money. It's their risk.
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Fiduciary duty, public money, and the one person nobody can route around
item.content:encoded:
Fair warning, saved this one for Saturday morning… About double the length of my usual essay. But I had some thoughts…

I saw one in a parking lot last week. You know the car. The one whose founder has spent the last two years becoming the story. This one still had its 30-day temporary tags.

Before I could stop myself, I said it out loud: You still thought that was a good idea?

I stand by it. A car is a purchase, and a purchase is a vote. Every new one adds value to a company whose largest shareholder is now the biggest known donor in these midterms. And it isn’t the only electric car anymore. Others exist now, many better, and to my eye this one has barely changed since it debuted. Buying it today means looking at the whole package, politics included, and deciding that’s fine.

A new Alex Gibney documentary about him includes a financial analyst who says the car company “is not automobile manufacturing or automobile retailing.” It’s closer to a religion, he argues. That explains the 30-day tags. People don’t buy into a religion on the specs.

The people I feel for bought theirs years ago, before he went all-in on politics. They bought a car. They didn’t sign up for a cause. Now some of them put stickers on the bumper explaining when they bought it. I can’t think of another car whose owners feel the need to publicly distance themselves from the company. The closest I can come is a certain fast-food chain with a very good chicken sandwich, and even its regulars don’t put disclaimers on their cars.

So there are two kinds of people in that parking lot: the ones who chose this, and the passengers who didn’t. This essay is about the passengers.

Leadership has an old word for this, and most people file it under compliance: fiduciary duty. A legal box for the general counsel. A clause nobody reads until something goes wrong.

I think of it as infrastructure. Fiduciary duty is the promise that your personal convictions won’t be paid for with other people’s exposure. It’s the load-bearing wall between what you own and what you’ve been trusted with. You don’t notice it while it holds. You notice it when someone starts knocking holes in it to make room for themselves.

The word comes from the Latin for trust, and that’s the whole idea. Anyone who leads something shared, a company, a budget, a team’s reputation, a public contract – is holding it in trust for people who aren’t in the room. The test isn’t whether a decision is legal. It’s simpler than that: who pays if you’re wrong? If the answer is anyone but you, it was never only your call.

A recent review of that documentary in The Atlantic put the danger in two sentences: “Delusions of grandeur are one thing. The real trouble comes when one person’s delusions become other people’s reality.” That’s fiduciary failure, defined by someone who wasn’t trying to define it.

So here’s a leadership teardown of a man I won’t name. You’ll recognize him anyway.

A disclosure before I start: I used to own stock in his car company. I sold every share and lived on it as severance when USAID cut my work during the reductions his efficiency office drove. So I’ve been a passenger too.

This is also the first time I’ve written about him at all. I’ve tried to stay objective by holding him to the same framework I use with every founder I coach, and by sticking to the record. Read what follows with all of that in mind.

The setup

Picture a founder whose largest single customer is the government. A Washington Post analysis counted at least $38 billion in public contracts, loans, subsidies, and tax credits across his companies. His space company, now publicly traded, gets about a fifth of its revenue from Washington. Super-voting shares give him 79% of the vote on a 42% economic stake.

This election cycle, he has put roughly $366 million of his own money into the midterms. There’s no real precedent for that. The $290 million he spent in 2024, when the White House was on the ballot, was already the record for any individual donor. The previous midterm record was $179 million, set by a Democratic megadonor in 2022. He has more than doubled it, with weeks still to go.

Put it in human terms. The most any one person can give a candidate this cycle is $3,500 per election, or $7,000 across a primary and a general. Matching his $366 million that way would require more than 52,000 Americans to each write the maximum check. He doesn’t have to, because he isn’t writing to candidates. He’s writing to super PACs, which can take unlimited sums. That’s how one person steps around a limit designed for everyone else.

To be clear, this essay isn’t about Citizens United. The ruling that opened the door to unlimited outside spending deserves its own argument, and that’s for another day. As far as I can tell, everything he has done here is legal.

But legal is the floor, not the standard. The law tells you what you can do with your own money. Fiduciary duty asks a harder question: who pays if you’re wrong? A leader can stay inside every rule and still move the risk of his bets onto people who never agreed to carry it. That isn’t a legal problem. It’s a leadership one.

There’s a quieter irony, too. Federal law bars government contractors from contributing to federal campaigns. His company can’t write that check. He can.

Follow the money

Most of it goes to the Senate. Here’s where his team says the money went JUST between July and September:

  • $158 million to the main super PAC for Senate Republicans. One of the largest known political donations in American history. On its own, it raised more than the Democrats’ Senate super PAC took in from all its donors that quarter.

  • $76 million to his own super PAC, which runs turnout in seven Senate battlegrounds and about three dozen House races. Its filings show it spent $16.6 million on Senate races by late September, led by Texas and Ohio.

  • $10 million to a super PAC backing one Senate candidate in Texas, where his space company is headquartered.

  • $32 million more to the House Republican super PAC, the Republican governors and the Republican attorneys general.

That’s only what’s disclosed. More has gone through groups that don’t name their donors.

Look closely at Texas, because that’s where his operation has been most focused. The candidate is the state’s attorney general. He took office in 2015 and was indicted that same year on felony securities fraud charges, accused of soliciting investors in a startup without disclosing his own financial stake in it. He pleaded not guilty, and the charges were eventually dismissed under a pretrial agreement that included $271,000 and 100 hours of community service. In 2023, his own party’s state House impeached him on articles alleging corruption and bribery. The state Senate acquitted him on all 16. This spring, he beat his party’s sitting senator in a runoff.

Senate Republicans’ main super PAC spent months reluctant to spend for him. Its own filing shows how that changed. On September 9, the founder gave it $75 million. The next day, it sent $75 million to a PAC backing the Texas candidate. On September 23, he gave $83 million. The next day, $83 million went to Texas. That Texas PAC spent more than $77 million on ads in September alone.

Pause on that. This essay is about fiduciary duty. The candidate getting the most attention from its subject was once charged with failing to tell investors about his own stake in their money.

Two senators his PAC has backed sit on the Appropriations Committee, which funds some of his company’s biggest contracts. One of them chairs it. Senators also confirm the people who run the agencies that buy his rockets, and they serve six-year terms, not two. If you want the most durable return on a political check, you write it to the Senate.

What does that do to a democracy? It doesn’t buy votes. It buys volume. Every race his money touches gets louder in one direction: more mailers, more door knocks, more ads, in what’s already projected to be the most expensive midterm ever, with a record $11.6 billion in political advertising. In a close Senate race, the side that can afford a bigger ground game in October can tip who shows up in November.

Big money in politics isn’t new, and it isn’t one-sided. The midterm record he just broke belonged to a left-wing donor. But there’s a difference between many wealthy donors pulling in different directions and one man, whose companies depend on the government, out-giving every donor to the other party’s Senate super PAC combined, in a single quarter. The first is a market. The second is a single point of failure.

What the last check bought

We’ve seen what this kind of spending buys. We saw it with less money.

After 2024, he got a desk inside the government and a mandate to cut it. His efficiency office went after budgets, staff, and contracts at all seven agencies where his own companies held contracts. The supplier suddenly audited his own customers from the inside.

The office closed this July. In August, the Government Accountability Office audited its claims. It couldn’t verify 96% of the reported savings from canceled grants. About $27 billion in “savings” was never executed. The office didn’t answer the auditors’ questions, and the White House says it won’t issue a final report. The website still claims $215 billion.

Who was minding the store?

Fiduciary duty runs in two directions. One is not spending other people’s risk. The other is simply showing up.

In early 2025, he headed six companies, including a public carmaker with millions of shareholders. He was also, by his own account to friends, sleeping in his government office a few minutes’ walk from the West Wing. He reportedly had a giant screen brought into that office so he could play video games. And the efficiency office he led was busy dismantling the country’s foreign aid agency, which he boasted he fed into a wood chipper.

That agency was never just a line item. A study published in The Lancet in July 2025 estimated that programs it funded prevented more than 91 million deaths over two decades. It projected that unless the cuts were reversed, they could lead to more than 14 million additional deaths by 2030, 4.5 million of them children under five. That’s a model’s projection, not a body count, and models can be wrong. But it is the fiduciary question at its starkest. Who pays if you’re wrong? Here, it isn’t shareholders. It’s people who will never know his name.

That spring, the carmaker reported a 71% drop in first-quarter profit and a 9% drop in revenue. Investors said out loud what the numbers implied: their CEO was distracted. Only then did he announce he’d step back from Washington.

He’s famous for his hours, and maybe he works more of them than anyone alive. But attention isn’t renewable. Even a genius gets the same 24 hours as everyone else, and every hour spent running a government office, or a video game, is an hour not spent on the companies whose shareholders are counting on him.

The games tell a small but revealing story. When gamers asked how he kept top-ranked characters while running six companies, he admitted others played his accounts for him. When you can’t do it all, you can hand the controller to someone else and keep your name on the leaderboard.

Shareholders can’t do that. They can’t hand off their exposure. In CLUTCH terms, he was a License holder who left one car idling in the driveway while he drove someone else’s, and the shareholders were still sitting in the passenger seat.

To be fair to him, many aerospace firms sell mostly to the government; the public market for rockets is small, and his company won many contracts by underbidding rivals.

None of that changes the problem’s shape. When one person ties a shared asset to a personal bet, the bet can be legal, sincere, even smart. It still moves the risk onto passengers. With 79% of the vote in one pair of hands, the other shareholders are in the back seat. The taxpayers aren’t even in the car.

The teardown: running him through CLUTCH

Most leadership advice treats leadership as a trait: you either have it or you don’t. CLUTCH treats it as a vehicle, a system of parts that have to work together. CREATE is the engine. VOICES is the gearbox. The 6C Compass is the navigation. DELEGATE is the handoff. And the part the book is named for holds it all together: “The connective tissue between all four is emotional intelligence, the clutch mechanism that enables smooth shifting between systems.”

The vehicle matters because of who’s riding in it. A solo driver can take whatever risks he likes. A driver with passengers owes them something, whether or not they get a say in the route.

Put this founder on the lift, and the diagnosis is the same at every station: a spectacular engine, one gear, a compass stuck on one heading, no handoff, and no clutch.

That isn’t a character study. The book is blunt that most leadership breakdowns “aren’t leadership problems. They’re design problems.” This one is a design problem: a trillion-dollar engine, one set of hands on the wheel, no brake on the passenger side, and a country full of passengers who never bought a ticket.

The engine: CREATE

The book calls CREATE “six cylinders of organizational capacity that must fire together”: Culture, Relationships, Execution, Agility, Teaching and Ethics. It’s blunt about what happens when they don’t: “When even one misfires, friction builds, capacity drops, and bottlenecks return.”

Two of his fire harder than almost anyone’s alive. Execution: rockets that land themselves and fly again. Agility: a satellite network switched on over a war zone within days of the invasion. Most leaders would trade a great deal for either one. Now listen to the other four.

  • Culture is designed. “Culture isn’t vibes. It’s designed.” When the person at the top treats shared assets as personal ones, he’s designing a culture where everyone below learns that’s how it works here.

  • Relationships are misfiring. Days after he left government, the president he’d spent $290 million to elect was publicly threatening to cancel his contracts. Now an ally is testing a workaround. And I’d bet plenty of early customers are tired of explaining their car.

  • Teaching is dead. The book’s line: “The point of leadership isn’t to create followers. It’s to CREATE more leaders.” The efficiency office closed with no final report and left nothing for the next team to learn from. An organization that won’t learn from its own record isn’t efficient. It’s just fast.

  • Ethics is knocking. Funding the senators who fund your contracts, and backing a candidate once charged with misleading investors, is a misfire you can hear from the street.

An engine running two cylinders at redline sounds powerful. It’s also exactly how engines blow, and when they do, the passengers feel it first.

The gearbox: VOICES

VOICES names six leadership presences: Visionary, Operator, Independent, Coach, Encourager, and Sculptor. The book’s diagnosis is simple: “Most leaders over-rely on one or two defaults.” Its prescription is harder: learn to “shift cleanly between all six gears.”

He has two defaults, and he redlines both. The Visionary says, Mars. The Operator sleeps on the factory floor, and later in a government office, because if he isn’t in the room, it isn’t happening. Those two gears built rockets that land. They also built organizations where nothing important moves without him.

The gears he skips are the ones that build other people. The Coach asks instead of tells. The Encourager builds belief. The Sculptor names the gap between where someone is and where they could be. Every one of those gears makes the leader a little less necessary. That’s the point, and it’s exactly the trade he won’t make.

The book is blunt about the cost: “leadership that stays locked in one gear creates dependence. Leadership that teaches others how to shift builds real capacity.” Look at who depends on him now: an ally’s army, his country’s space program, shareholders who can’t outvote him, and a party’s Senate campaign. That isn’t capacity. It’s a single point of failure with a gas pedal.

A leader stuck in one gear at highway speed isn’t bold. He’s stuck, and so is everyone riding with him.

The navigation: the 6C Compass

The book calls the 6C Compass “a decision-rights framework that clarifies who decides, how, and when.” It has six modes: Command, Consultative, Collaborative, Consensus, Core Expert, and Choice. “None of the six is better than the others. Each is correct for a specific kind of terrain.” The skill is reading the terrain, and a compass stuck on one heading can’t.

Command, used well. Command is for moments “where speed and safety demand you decide and move.” One early reader called it a fire extinguisher: essential, and rarely pulled. Switching the network on in the first days of the war was exactly the moment to pull the fire extinguisher. This year he shut down the invader’s unauthorized use of it, and Ukraine’s former defense minister credited the call with protecting the country’s air defenses and sparing thousands of civilian lives. Credit where it’s due.

Command, past its expiry date. Whether that network can be used over enemy territory touches an ally’s war plan and a government’s foreign policy. That’s Consultative at minimum: he can still make the call, but he asks the people who will live with it first. Instead, it sits on one desk. He reportedly sees it as escalation. Kyiv argues it would shorten the war. So Kyiv has started testing an alternative with a European partner. That’s what a team does when one person holds a switch it can’t live without. It quietly builds a workaround. A fire extinguisher that never gets put down isn’t safety. It’s a flood.

Command, with no name on it. This week Ukraine says its military terminals were throttled overnight, without warning, for anything moving faster than 100 miles an hour, the speed of the drones it uses to intercept Russia’s. Zelenskyy called it “a big mistake” that “will bring a lot of human losses.” Asked who made the call, the founder said such limits are “decided by the US military and ultimately” the president. The White House has neither confirmed nor denied it. A Republican senator wants the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate. Maybe it really was Washington’s call. That’s the point. A decision this consequential, on a system this many people depend on, now has no visible owner. The Compass exists to answer one question before any other: who decides? When the answer is a shrug and a pointed finger, the passengers can’t even tell who’s driving.

Choice, mislabeled. His defenders will say the political money is Choice: his money, his call. The book frames Choice as handing over the keys, and keys come with guardrails, because a decision is only truly yours when its consequences stay with you. When they land on shareholders who can’t outvote him and taxpayers who fund his contracts, it’s no longer Choice. It’s Command over other people’s risk with a Choice label stuck on the front.

Core Expert, missing. The Core Expert mode asks one question: “Who’s best positioned to decide this?” Thousands of grant and contract cuts later, the auditors couldn’t verify most of the savings, and nearly 2,000 contracts the office said it had ended were never actually terminated. From the outside, it doesn’t look like anyone asked.

Map his biggest calls on the Compass and almost all of them land in one mode. A compass stuck on Command doesn’t point north. It points at him.

The handoff: DELEGATE

DELEGATE starts by separating the Title from the License. The Title is final accountability, and the leader keeps it. The License is operational ownership, and the leader hands it off. Then it breaks every handoff into eight parts: Define the Win, Establish the Way, List the Guardrails, Expect the Process, Give the Right Support, Agree on Checkpoints, Transfer Ownership, and Encourage Growth. Skip one, and the work comes back.

Run him through it, and he fails in both directions: as the person holding a License, and as the person handed one.

First, the License he holds. He has Title to his fortune. He holds only a License to his space company’s relationship with its largest customer, a relationship the shareholders own and the public paid to build. A License comes with guardrails. When the License holder starts acting like the Title holder, there’s no one left to enforce them. With 79% of the vote, nobody else has to agree. The same Atlantic review described power like his as “so complete that it becomes self-ratifying.” In CLUTCH terms, that’s a car with no brake on the passenger side.

Then the License he was handed. Put the efficiency office through the eight parts and count the gaps. Define the Win: its own savings tally kept growing, from $55 billion to $215 billion, and the auditors couldn’t verify most of it. List the Guardrails: it went after contracts at the very agencies that paid his companies. Agree on Checkpoints: it didn’t answer the auditors. Transfer Ownership: it closed with no final report and nothing handed on. From the outside, that’s half the handoff missing, in public.

Delegation that comes back wasn’t delegation. It was a loan. This one came back unaudited, and the taxpayers are still holding the note.

The clutch: emotional intelligence

“The clutch is what lets you pause between stimulus and response.” It lets a leader feel the engine and the road at the same time and shift without grinding metal.

Here’s the strange part: the self-awareness was there. In May he said he’d spend a lot less on politics. In July he said he’d gotten carried away and too involved. Then, starting that same month, $276 million came in.

That’s what a missing clutch looks like. The driver can hear the gears grinding. He just can’t stop pressing the accelerator.

The one in your building

Most leaders will never write a nine-figure check. But most organizations have a smaller version of this person. The founder who keeps the biggest client relationship in his own phone. The department head who spends the team’s reputation on a personal fight. The executive who cashes the board’s trust on a pet project. And behind each of them, a row of passengers.

Put your own leadership on the lift this week:

  1. CREATE. Which cylinder are you ignoring because the loud ones are firing so well?

  2. VOICES. Which gear haven’t you used in a month, and what has that cost the people around you?

  3. 6C Compass. Which decision are you calling Choice that is really Command over someone else’s risk?

  4. DELEGATE. Is the line between your Title and your License written down anywhere?

  5. The clutch. What have you already admitted you got wrong, and kept doing anyway?

The book’s last word on this is the hopeful one: “The bottleneck isn’t a character flaw. It’s a design problem.” Character is slow to change. Design isn’t.

So look at the one in your building. Look at the passengers. Then ask the question I blurted out in that parking lot: You still think that’s a good idea?

Every station on that lift is a chapter in the book.

CLUTCH gives you CREATE, VOICES, the 6C Compass, and DELEGATE, built to work together, each with its own diagnostic, so the line between what you keep and what you hand off stops living in one person’s head.

item.title: The room laughed
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: A congressman, a diesel question, and why the honest answer has to reach the people who asked
item.content:encoded:
“The facts are diesel prices have gone up,” the congressman said. “There’s no question about it. Why has it gone up? Because the Democrats’ environmental regulations have not...”

The room laughed before he could finish.

That was Tuesday night in Cambridge, Maryland, at a League of Women Voters forum. Rep. Andy Harris was debating his Democratic challenger, Dan Schwartz, on the administration’s deal to buy diesel from Russia. When the audience laughed, Harris told a woman she was rude. Someone else called back, “You started it.”

This was not a hostile crowd. It was his own district, one he has held since 2011 and one that leans conservative.

This isn’t an essay about who is right on fuel policy. Both parties are playing the blame game on prices this fall. What interests me is the laugh. A room in a district that leans his way heard an explanation that didn’t match what they were paying at the pump, and they said so before he could finish.

That laugh is the sound of credibility running out. I’ve heard it in boardrooms, faculty meetings, and all-hands calls. Usually it’s silent. Here is my argument: when a cost is visible to everyone, your explanation stops being a message and becomes a test. People will forgive a hard truth. They will not forgive being asked to unsee what is in front of them. Leaders who fail that test rarely lack the honest answer. They just give it to the wrong room.

What the room could see

In September, US diesel hit a record about $6.53 a gallon, nearly double the roughly $3.70 it cost a year earlier. The federal Energy Information Administration points to tight diesel markets, high crude prices and constrained oil flows from the Middle East, and international analysts add lost refining in Russia. On the Shore, people had paid that number themselves, in tractors, workboats and trucks.

Regulation may well play some part in what fuel costs. That’s a fair debate. The room wouldn’t accept a single cause, sitting on the other side of the aisle, when the government’s own analysts tie the price to a global squeeze.

People can take a hard truth: prices are up, it hurts, here’s what we’re doing about it. They won’t take an explanation that insults what they can see for themselves.

Candor to the wrong room

After the forum, Harris told reporters he thinks the Russia diesel deal is a mistake. That’s a real position, and not an easy one to take about your own party’s administration.

It’s also not what the room heard. On stage: it’s because of them. Off stage: this decision was a mistake.

Blame looks backward and outward. It finds the cause in the past and in someone else. Accountability looks forward and inward. It names a choice your own side made and says what should change.

Here’s what matters for the rest of us. The honest answer existed. He gave it the same evening. He gave it to reporters instead of the people who came to ask.

Accountability you only offer in private isn’t accountability. It’s a confession to the wrong audience.

Most leaders know this split. The all-hands gets the market, the budget, the board. The one colleague you trust gets “we got it wrong.” The team that needed the second version gets the first.

The bill shows up everywhere except where it started

Diesel is an odd kind of cost. Most people never buy it. It sits inside the price of everything that rides on a truck, from groceries to lumber. It never appears on your receipt, and you pay it on almost every line.

Low trust works the same way inside an organization. It shows up as the meeting that needed a pre-meeting, the sign-off that took a month, the strong performer who left without saying much about why. And the “it’s because of them” answer is one of the fastest ways to run up that bill, even when it’s partly true, because the people in front of you can see it isn’t the whole story.

What it costs when they stop believing you

I once worked in an organization where the head, several rungs above me, kept saying he would do something. He said it more than once. Then nothing happened, and he never followed through. I still don’t know why it wasn’t done. There was no explanation at all, good or bad, and the silence did the same work a bad one would have. After a while, you couldn’t believe him when he made any other declaration.

Your people don’t stop listening. They start translating. Every announcement gets a second meaning in the hallway afterward, and the bad news stops reaching you early.

Then the day comes when you have a hard truth that really is outside your control, and it lands with the same discount. You spent the credibility you needed on an explanation you didn’t.

Build it so blame has nowhere to land

Blame isn’t mainly a character flaw. It thrives wherever nothing in how the team runs asks for anything else. Three pieces of infrastructure change that.

  1. A standing slot for the visible bad news. Open the meeting with what everyone can already see – costs, morale, the slipped date – said plainly, before anyone has to ask. Stating the obvious earns you the right to be believed about what isn’t.

  2. Decisions with names on them. Record who decided what, and when. Once you write down the owner, “it’s because of them” has nowhere to hide, not even from you.

  3. No explanation without a next step. Every account of what went wrong ships with what happens now and when the team will hear again. Blame ends the conversation. Accountability schedules the next one.

The laugh in Cambridge made the news. The one on your team never will, because they stopped laughing out loud long ago. This week, the question worth sitting with is whether they’ve also stopped believing you.

Accountability is something you build into how a team runs, not a speech you give after things go wrong.

item.title: The Ship of Theseus problem
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Are you getting credit for your ideas?
item.content:encoded:
Plutarch tells of the ship Theseus sailed home from Crete. The Athenians kept it for centuries, replacing each rotten plank with new timber, until philosophers began to argue: if they replaced every plank, was it still his ship? This month, book publishers walked into the same question, and so will every team handed a new tool.

The story, briefly

Recently, WIRED’s Adam Morgan spoke anonymously with more than two dozen staff at HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette. His research uncovered that chatbots drafted publicity and back-cover copy, cover art, marketing materials, and emails to literary agents, often at executives’ request, rarely with disclosure or the author’s consent.

At HarperCollins, leaders bought the AI licenses first. Then dozens of staff were, in Morgan’s word, “voluntold” to become AI Champions and find uses in monthly sessions. Simon & Schuster ran a use-case contest in May 2024 with a $10,000 top prize, then pulled back after complaints, and staff organized a letter against workflow-monitoring software. Hachette says AI is for operations, not creative work, a line the reporting suggests doesn’t hold in practice. All of this on teams cut to five or six people handling two or three times as many books. One agent, Emma Dries, asked for something simple: tell us which tools you use, and when.

Whose work is it?

Beneath the publishing story is a question every team will face. When a tool touches the work, who gets the credit?

Look at France. Last month the Académie Goncourt pulled Thélyson Orélien’s bestselling debut novel from its prize list after an anonymous account ran passages through an AI detector. Orélien, a Haitian-Canadian writer, denies it. He says he used tools for research on foreign idioms and that “not a single sentence” came from a machine. He has also admitted to plagiarism in earlier writing. Detectors are disputed, and some critics have asked whether Caribbean speech rhythms simply read as machine-made to a machine. I don’t know what’s true. I suspect the people who decided don’t either.

That’s the point. Nobody agreed on the line before the work was done, so an algorithm and an anonymous account drew it afterward, in public. Credit went to whoever spoke first.

I’ll admit this one gets personal. I write novels, and the idea that anyone can sit down with a chatbot and ask it for the next great American novel makes me prickly. So I’ve had to ask myself why.

Art is a series of decisions. What color. How much pressure on the brush. Which word, which scene to cut. Those decisions come from some talent, a lot of experience with the medium, and more reps and revisions than anyone ever sees. A tool can offer options. It can’t make the decisions for you, and it can’t do the reps. So if a writer uses one, how is that different from using it for anything else? It comes down to ownership of the ideas. Whose decisions are on the page?

Which is why I’ll confess to a fair amount of schadenfreude reading about the publishers. This is an industry, prizes included, that publicly shames writers suspected of using AI, sometimes on the word of a detector that is itself an AI, while quietly running its own copy through chatbots. I couldn’t put that irony in a novel. An editor would cut it as too neat.

And it raises an uncomfortable question for me. I use a grammar checker, because grammar has never been my strength. Fixing a comma is one thing. Accepting a suggestion that rewrites my sentence is another. I’m on Theseus’s ship too. If I accept enough small fixes, is it still my sentence? My answer is that the ship belongs to whoever chooses the course. The idea and the argument are mine. But I’d rather say that here than have a detector say it for me.

So if art is a series of decisions, maybe AI is just another tool of creation, like the brush, the camera or the word processor. Painters were told photography would kill painting. Instead it freed them from copying the world and pushed them toward what only they could see. The tool was never the threat. The threat is handing it the decisions and keeping the byline. A chatbot can offer a thousand next sentences. Choosing the one that belongs on the page, and answering for it, is still the work, and still the credit.

The publishing staff is on the same edge. A publicist who writes a sharp pitch now has to wonder whether the agent thinks a chatbot wrote it. Undisclosed use quietly takes credit from everyone who did the work themselves.

Three mistakes, in CLUTCH terms

In CLUTCH, every piece of work carries a title and a license. The title is final accountability: the leader who answers for it when it goes out the door. Note: in this sense, not a book title, but a car’s title. The license is operational ownership: who actually makes the calls. Whoever makes the decisions holds the license, on a page or in a company. When both are clear, credit is clear. Every mistake in the publishing story blurs the two.

  • The tool came before the problem. Buying first quietly turns the job from “solve our problem” into “justify our purchase.” Monthly sessions to find uses are the tell. Nobody brainstorms uses for a fix they asked for.

  • The mandate traveled down without the license. The champions were handed a job and no authority: not whether a use was appropriate, not whether authors should be told, not whether the honest answer was “nowhere.” DELEGATE exists to stop exactly this, a handoff where the work moves and the decision stays put. What follows is drift, private calls nobody decided, and the bottleneck: every real decision routed back up.

  • The people whose names were on the line were never told. The executives held the title and made the call. The authors’ names went on the covers, and nobody told them what they touched in the work published under their names. And staff objections, the cheapest risk data a company ever gets, were treated as a cost of doing business.

What to do instead

If you’re about to introduce anything new, a platform, a process, a chatbot, decide who’s steering before you start swapping planks.

  • Start from the problem. Name it before you buy anything. “Our teams carry three times the titles” is a problem. “We have licenses” is not.

  • Give champions a real license. Write down what they can decide without asking, including the right to rule out a use. Use the 6C Compass to say the decision type out loud: is this your command, a consultation, or genuinely theirs?

  • Treat objections as data. Log them, answer them in writing, and show what changed because of them. If nothing ever changes, people stop telling you.

  • Write the credit line before the work. For anything that leaves the building, three questions: whose idea was it, who decided, and what tools touched it? Tell the people whose names are on it. Disclosure costs a paragraph. An accusation after the fact costs far more.

Philosophers have argued about Theseus’s ship for two thousand years and still haven’t settled it. Your team doesn’t have that long. Someone will decide whose work this is: either you, in writing, before the tool goes in, or an algorithm and an anonymous account afterward. Leadership is infrastructure. Decide who’s steering, tell the people whose names are on the line, and a new tool is just another plank. So, are you getting credit for your ideas? Only if someone decided, out loud and in advance, who chooses the course.

Matt Goode is the founder of Goode Design & Consulting, where he helps founders and school leaders build leadership that keeps working when they step away. He spent twenty years in the classroom, built leadership benches at USAID, and writes fiction as m kirk, where he still chooses the course.

Who decides, who is told, whose name goes on it.

item.title: Don’t Hire the Eagle Scout. Build the Patrol.
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: The badge isn’t what makes Scouts lead. The system underneath it is.
item.content:encoded:
A couple of summers ago at Philmont, my son was our crew’s navigator for the day. It was first thing in the morning, everyone keen to get moving, and he blew past a couple of obvious markers and missed a trail turn. I had a choice: Scouter uniform or dad hat. I kept the uniform on and said nothing.

Two miles later, the crew hit something they couldn’t ignore: a dirt road. They weren’t technically lost. They weren’t where they were supposed to be. Then the looks came, all pointed at me. Why didn’t you say something?

The detour cost us four extra miles, most of it in ankle-deep mud. My son took the ribbing. When we debriefed as a crew, we found out someone had spotted the trailhead and kept quiet, and that morning eagerness had outrun everyone’s judgment. For the rest of the trek, they checked every landmark. We didn’t get lost again.

My son forgave me. Kinda.

Earlier this month, Scouting America field director Blake Nettleton argued that employers should pay attention to Eagle Scouts. He cites a 2026 Harris Poll study of 3,178 U.S. adults. Seventy-four percent of Eagle Scouts have held a leadership position at work. Among adults who never joined Scouting, that number is 31 percent.

I believe those numbers. I just don’t think they say what we want them to say.

The badge is the wrong signal

Blake’s piece compares Eagle Scouts with people who never joined. But the study had a third group, Scouts who never made Eagle, and that’s where it gets interesting. If you broaden the question to leadership roles at work, in the community, or in the military, 80 percent of Eagle Scouts say yes. So do 71 percent of Scouts who stopped short. Among people who never joined, it’s 38 percent.

I’m one of the 71 percent. I never earned Eagle. At the age I should have been finishing it, I chased swimming cuts to become a more competitive Division I prospect. I swam in college, met my wife, and made friends for life. Zero regrets.

With one giant asterisk. I never finished the paperwork for my Eagle because, at the time, I didn’t value it. Once you turn 18, that door closes for good.

But the badge is the only thing I left behind. What I learned as a Scout, and as a leader of other Scouts, came with me anyway.

There’s a catch. Scouting America paid for the survey, and it’s a snapshot, not a trial. Families who sign up may differ from families who don’t.

If the badge adds so little on top of the program, it’s the wrong thing to hire for. What’s worth stealing is the machine underneath it.

What a patrol actually is

Strip out the uniforms, and a troop is a four-part leadership system.

A small team with a real job. Six to eight Scouts who have to eat, pitch tents, and get the gear home. Failure is visible by dinner.

Authority sits with the learner. The patrol leader is a teenager, chosen by peers who don’t have to follow. Nobody is paid to comply.

Adults aren’t allowed to rescue. When I was a Scout, adults mostly stayed in the background. I can remember them stepping in exactly twice.

The first time, a younger Scout picked up a copperhead. Yes, picked it up. The second was a winter campout on the Appalachian Trail, when one of us slid into hypothermia. Both times, the adults moved fast, and both ended in some kind of evacuation.

Everything else was ours. The plans, the meals, the routes, the arguments about all three. We made plenty of mistakes, and nobody stepped in to stop them, because none of them could really hurt us. That wasn’t neglect. It was room, and someone had decided exactly how much of it we could safely have. I didn’t see the design then. I see it now. Short of a copperhead or hypothermia, my job as Scoutmaster is to advise and keep my hands in my pockets, even when I could fix the plan in thirty seconds.

Reps on a cadence. A weekly meeting, a monthly outing, for years. A Tufts study of Philadelphia Cub Scouts found that those who showed up regularly scored higher on character measures than those who didn’t. The dose matters.

None of that is a curriculum. It’s structure, and it runs whether anyone feels inspired that week or not.

What most companies do instead

Now look at how most organizations make a first-time manager. Promote the best individual contributor, send them to a two-day course, and hand them a team and a boss who steps in the moment anything wobbles.

Then watch what happens when something goes sideways. At Philmont, someone on the crew saw the trailhead and kept quiet, because the map belonged to the navigator. Teams do the same thing every week. The person who spots the problem says nothing because it isn’t their call, and the boss fixes it before anyone has to learn from it.

That’s training. It’s an event. The patrol is infrastructure.

Scouting keeps adults from leading. Most companies quietly pull them back in, then wonder why their new managers stall.

Build the patrol

You don’t need a merit badge program. You need four honest answers about every person you’re developing.

  1. Do they own an outcome that fails visibly if they drop it?

  2. Do they hold real authority over the work, even if it’s borrowed?

  3. Has their manager agreed, out loud, not to rescue them?

  4. Will they get another rep within a month?

A no on any of these means you aren’t developing a leader. You’re hosting one.

Score your team on all four in two minutes with The Patrol Check.

The leaders you already employ

Blake’s best point is his last one. The den leaders, Scoutmasters, and committee chairs on your payroll run this system on their weekends. Every month, they practice advising instead of doing, the exact skill most senior people never build.

You may not need to hire the Eagle Scout. You may already employ the adult who helped make one. Ask them how they do it, then ask why your org makes it so hard.

Stop recruiting for the badge. Build the patrol. Then let them miss the turn.

Matt Goode is the founder of Goode Design & Consulting, where he helps founders and school leaders build leadership that keeps working when they step away. He spent twenty years in the classroom and is Scoutmaster of two troops in the Baltimore Area Council, where the hardest part of the job is keeping his hands in his pockets.

item.title: Accountability isn't an event
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Leaders and their managers agree on what leaders are worst at. Knowing hasn't fixed it
item.category: Winning feels like a near miss
item.content:encoded:
Leaders and the managers who report to them disagree about almost everything Gallup measured. They agree on one thing: what leaders are worst at.

In a new Gallup study, Jim Harter and Corey Tatel asked both groups to rate leaders on seven competencies: building relationships, developing people, leading change, inspiring others, thinking critically, communicating clearly, and creating accountability. Creating accountability came last. For both groups.

46% of leaders rate themselves exceptional or outstanding at it.

30% of managers say the same about their own leader.

That 16-point gap sounds large until you see the rest. On six of the seven competencies, managers rate their leaders at least 20 points below the leaders’ own ratings. Accountability is where the two groups come closest.

So leaders still overrate themselves here, just by less than anywhere else. They can see the weakness. Their managers see it too. And seeing it hasn’t fixed it.

The problem isn’t awareness

That matters for how organizations try to fix it. Most develop managers through events: a two-day course, an assessment, a box checked before the budget year closes. A course can teach a skill. It can’t make one stick. And you can’t train your way out of a weakness everyone in the room can already see.

What I hear when leaders describe accountability

I coach about 20 executives and work with about 10 organizations. When I ask a senior leader how they hold their managers accountable, the answer almost always arrives as a story about a moment. A missed quarter. A hard conversation. A performance plan.

Almost nobody describes a Tuesday.

That’s the tell. Accountability, as most leaders practice it, happens after something has already gone wrong. So the manager on the other side only meets it when something is broken. In schools, it even has a season. Department chairs and division heads meet accountability at evaluation time, and the rest of the year it lives in good intentions.

The band doesn’t get tight at the clinic

Any working musician knows the difference between a clinic and a rehearsal. I used to play in a faculty band and work with student bands after school. A clinic teaches you something. Rehearsal is where the band actually locks in, every week, in a room where nobody is paying. The part I always loved was the listening. Everyone in the ensemble listens to everyone else, for cues, for tuning, for knowing you’re in the refrain and not the bridge. That’s where the dragged tempo and the missed change get fixed, while they’re small and cheap.

Last month, U2 marked fifty years together by going back to the Dublin school where it started. In September 1976, a 14-year-old drummer pinned a note to the school noticeboard, and a few classmates with limited musical experience turned up for a first practice in his family’s kitchen. Fifty years later, the same four played the schoolyard, with students from the school on strings. I don’t know what happens in their rehearsal room. But I know what it takes to keep the same four people in one band for half a century, and it isn’t a clinic. It’s decades of listening to each other.

A band that only plays together on stage finds its problems in front of an audience.

Most organizations run accountability the same way. There’s no weekly room where leaders and managers listen for each other’s cues, so the first time a manager hears the standard clearly is the night it matters, with everyone watching. The course was the clinic. Nobody booked the rehearsal room.

Gallup’s earlier work on why performance management fails shows how common this is: only 50% of employees clearly know what is expected of them at work. One reader summed it up for me in a single line: “A core leadership issue- clarity of expectations horizontally and vertically.” Half the band is guessing the set list. No wonder the accountability conversation feels like an ambush on one side and a necessary evil on the other.

What rehearsal looks like

Gallup’s prescription reads like a rehearsal plan, and it’s just as unglamorous: weekly manager conversations that combine coaching, recognition, priority-setting and discussion of individual strengths. Accountability as a regular, fair discipline, not something saved for corrective moments. The earlier piece sets a specific floor: meaningful feedback every week, substantial developmental coaching every month. Every rehearsal, and a proper lesson once a month.

Start with the set list. Agree on the one or two priorities that matter before you meet again, in words you’d both write down the same way.

Then work the hard passage. Ask what’s stuck, and stay on that one thing instead of touring every project. Coaching is a question about a specific problem, not a speech about general improvement.

Nod when someone nails the fill. Name one thing that went well last week, specifically enough that they could do it again on purpose. Vague recognition sounds like politeness. Specific recognition tells people what the standard is.

Write the parts for the players you have. Once a month, go deeper: ask where their work draws on what they do best and where it grinds against it. Sometimes the fix is adjusting the part, not pushing the player.

And close by checking this week’s set list against last week’s. If the same priority keeps showing up unplayed, that’s the conversation to have now, while it’s still a missed change and not a trainwreck on stage.

What changes when it becomes weekly

Marcel Schwantes flagged this research in Inc. this month, under a headline about how most companies train managers once. The number that should change that habit: the 30% of managers who rate their leader exceptional at accountability are three times as likely to be engaged, 51% versus 17%. These are survey ratings, not performance outcomes, so it’s an association, not proof. But it’s hard to wave away a gap that wide.

In my own work, the shift I see when accountability moves from reaction to rhythm is less dramatic than people expect, and more durable. It stops being a verdict and becomes maintenance. Recognition and correction travel through the same channel, so the correction doesn’t arrive from a stranger. Managers learn what good looks like before they’re judged on it.

One CEO I wrote about in CLUTCH ran a $50 million business with 120 employees and couldn’t take a vacation without his laptop. The first ritual we designed together was small: in his weekly 1:1s, he had to ask three questions before offering a single suggestion.

“What have you already tried?”

“What’s your instinct here?”

“What would you do if I weren’t available to ask?”

He hated it at first. It felt slow. Then one day his CFO said something that stopped him cold: “I’ve started actually preparing for our 1:1s now. I used to bring you problems. Now I bring you options.”

This is why I keep saying leadership is infrastructure, not training. The course isn’t useless. I run professional development sessions too, as every consultant does. But the session was never the system. The real consulting is building structures that keep running after I leave. The system is what happens on an ordinary Tuesday, when nothing is on fire, and you still sit down with the person who manages your people.

One thing to try this week

Most founders assume their expectations are obvious. Here’s how to find out in twenty minutes.

Pick the manager whose work you feel least sure about. Book 20 minutes with them before Friday. Open with one question: “In your own words, what do you think I expect of you this month?” Then listen the way a band listens. Don’t correct them while they talk. Write it down.

Then tell them what you would have said.

Put the two answers side by side. Where they match, say so out loud, because that’s recognition with a standard attached. Where they don’t, that’s the work. Before you leave, agree on one sentence you’d both write down the same way, and read it back to each other.

Then put the next conversation on the calendar for the same time next week. Not because something went wrong. Because that’s when rehearsal is.

U2’s fifty years started with one practice in a kitchen. This is yours.

You’ve just booked the rehearsal room.

item.title: What the auditors couldn't count
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: A watchdog can count awards and positions. It can't count what the people in those positions knew
item.content:encoded:
On September 30, the Government Accountability Office, Congress’s nonpartisan watchdog, published its review of what happened to American foreign assistance after USAID closed.

Most of the report is counting. Between January 2025 and March 2026, about 6,780 of 7,510 USAID awards were terminated. USAID’s workforce went from about 13,600 people worldwide to 241.

Two findings stopped me, and neither of them is a number.

The State Department, which now runs what remains, could not produce data on its own staffing levels during the eleven months the auditors asked for it. It also could not show written guidance, including standards, for how foreign assistance decisions get made.

Read that as an operator. An organization responsible for about $52 billion in active awards could not say who works there or how it decides.

I worked at BHA, USAID’s Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance. I’m not going to argue here about whether the agency should have closed. That’s a policy question, and you have your own view. I want to look at something narrower, because I see it in every kind of organization I work with, from Series B startups to independent schools.

What an audit can’t see

An audit counts what it can count: awards, dollars, positions. It can’t count what the people in those positions knew.

The USAID Employee Support Fund tried. They surveyed their members, and 225 answered. Health officers, agriculture and environment officers, governance specialists, economists, engineers, and the contracting officers who oversaw how the money was spent.

A third of all respondents are unemployed. Of those working again, nearly half have left the field entirely, and about one in four are still in international development or foreign affairs.

The health officers make it concrete. Of the 26 who answered, two still work in international development. Eight have changed fields entirely.

It’s a self-selected sample, not a census. But the direction is hard to miss. The awards moved to State. The knowledge didn’t move with them.

The contracting officer is the control system

Take the contracting officers. On an org chart, a contracting officer looks like administration. In practice, that’s the person who knows why a clause exists, which partner has quietly missed three reports, where the money legally can’t go, and what happened the last time someone tried.

Those are the organization’s controls. They live in someone’s head.

That’s what connects the GAO’s two findings. When the people who made the judgment leave, nothing remains to explain how decisions were made. The GAO warns that, without documented standards, officials risk decisions that are “inconsistent, ad hoc, or inefficient.” Not because the people still there are careless, but because they never wrote the standards down. They didn’t need to be. The people were the standards.

Fast to drain, slow to fill

You probably haven’t lost 98 percent of your staff. But you’ve seen the smaller version. A founder’s first operations hire leaves and takes the vendor history with her. A school loses a division head of twenty years, and the new one discovers the schedule runs on rules nobody wrote down.

What drained wasn’t only oversight. It was application. The officer who knows which roads wash out in the rainy season, so the food has to move by June. The agriculture specialist who remembers which seed variety failed in that valley, and why. The health officer who knows which district clinic reports its numbers on time and which one needs a phone call and a visit. None of that sits in an award file. It’s the difference between money that was spent and money that worked.

Systems thinkers call this a stock. Knowledge accumulates slowly, through years of flow: projects, mistakes, relationships, the third time you see the same problem. A restructuring can drain the stock in an afternoon. Refilling it runs at the original speed, because the only way to learn which roads flood is to be there when they do. That asymmetry is the whole story, and it’s true at any scale.

Headcount is just where the stock happens to be stored. Cut the headcount, and you’ve drained the stock, whether the spreadsheet shows it or not.

Hiring costs more than growing

The Fund put it plainly: “A government cannot buy it back with a hiring announcement.” Neither can a company, and there’s data on why.

Wharton’s Matthew Bidwell studied people hired from outside against people promoted from within into similar jobs. External hires were paid about 18 to 20 percent more, scored lower on performance reviews in their first two years, and were more likely to leave. What they lacked wasn’t talent. It was the firm-specific knowledge and relationships that only time inside builds.

You pay a premium to hire judgment from outside, then wait two years for it to work. Or you grow it, and keep it.

Before you cut, map the load

If you’re about to restructure, ask four questions first.

  1. Which three decisions stall if this person leaves on Friday? If you can’t name them, you don’t know what you’re cutting.

  2. Who else could make each of those calls today, without asking? If the answer is nobody, you’ve found a load-bearing wall.

  3. Who is learning those calls right now? If nobody is, every resignation becomes a restructuring you didn’t plan.

  4. How long would it take you to list who works for you, where they work, and what they own? The State Department couldn’t do it in eleven months. Your answer should be a day.

None of this needs a consultant. It needs someone willing to look at the building before taking out walls.

The GAO made three recommendations to State. Two of them come down to this: know who works for you, and write down how you decide. That advice holds for any organization, whatever its size or mission.

Leadership is infrastructure, not training.

item.title: The manuscript is not the bottleneck
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.content:encoded:
I recently finished a novel that was fine. Competent sentences, a plot that moved, a few scenes I would have cut. Before the author had even finished the manuscript, it had sold film rights. It was a first novel.

I closed it and asked the question every self-published writer asks eventually, usually late at night: how did that happen? Or more precisely: why hasn’t that happened for me?!

Luck? Skill? Both, in proportions nobody publishes.

I’m not asking out of bitterness. Well, not only. If you read this Substack, you know my lane: I help founders build the systems their companies run on. That’s my day job, as I call it. But self-publishing, under my own name and under my pen name, has turned out to be almost like starting a second company. OK, it is starting a second company. Maybe a third.

I’ve put two books into the world through my own imprints, and a third is finished and waiting on its first readers. What I’ve learned is the thing the writing workshops skip. Self-publishing doesn’t make you an author. It makes you a founder. The book is the product. Everything after the last page is distribution, operations, and sales, run by a team of one. Last week I wrote about how I systemized my own work, and this is why, in addition to growing Goode Design & Consulting, I accidentally started a second (or third) company: my nascent publishing empire. I needed a system to run on.

The Martian started as a blog

Andy Weir is the patron saint of people like me. He was a software engineer whose earlier attempt at a novel went nowhere with agents. So he posted The Martian on his own website, chapter by chapter, for free. Readers asked for an ebook. He put it on Kindle for 99 cents, the lowest price Amazon allowed, and it climbed the charts. Then an agent called. Then Crown. Then Fox. Then Matt Damon.

Notice what his readers were doing along the way. They weren’t just reading. They were emailing him corrections to his orbital math. By the time a publisher noticed, a crowd of people already had a stake in that book. That isn’t discovery. That’s a founder with early customers.

People tell Weir’s story as proof that quality rises. Read it again. He built an audience, and the audience did the discovering. The publisher wasn’t betting on Weir. It was buying a result.

The billionaire version

This week The New Yorker reviewed MacKenzie Scott’s new novel, Last Days in Two Nations, which she published in installments on Substack. Plenty of people have wondered aloud why she skipped Amazon. I don’t think it needs much of an explanation.

The review was rough on the craft. But The New Yorker reviewed a self-published, serialized novel, which is more attention than most of us will get in a lifetime. When your name already does the distributing, you can afford to walk away from the biggest bookstore on earth.

The review’s sharper point is that she couldn’t fully escape it anyway. Kindle Direct Publishing built the road most self-published fiction now travels, and even a writer stepping around Amazon is walking through the landscape it made. I’m on that road too. So is every indie author I know. The difference is that most of us don’t get to choose.

Each book taught the next one

Here’s what the founder’s job has looked like, one book at a time. Each one taught me something I used on the next.

  • Balance taught me that a reader is not a review. My first novel, published as m kirk, found good early readers. Then I learned that Amazon doesn’t treat every review the same, and a free early copy can quietly cost you one, no matter how much someone loved it. I had about 20 early readers for Balance, and most of their reviews didn’t show up – they shared them with me – because they never bought the book. I gifted them a copy. Amazon tracks it. I also learned I didn’t own the book’s ISBN, the thirteen-digit number bookstores and libraries use to find it. I’d taken Amazon’s free one, which can’t leave Amazon. Getting the paperback into bookstores and libraries now takes a second distributor and a second ISBN. None of that is writing. All of it decides whether anyone reads.

  • CLUTCH is where I applied those lessons, and found new ways to trip. It’s my leadership book, published under my own name. This time I bought my own block of ISBNs from Bowker, the agency that issues them, so the book’s identity belongs to me, not to Amazon. I launched it at $9.99 to get copies and reviews moving. Then I went live before registering the ISBN, so for its first week on sale, CLUTCH was missing from the catalog booksellers search. I didn’t know I’d missed a step until I went looking. On Amazon, the publisher line reads “m kirk,” my fiction pen name, because of one field Amazon locks the moment you hit publish. Changing it means a support case. That mistake sent me down a road I hadn’t heard of a few months ago: imprints, the publisher name printed on a book’s copyright page and carried in every bookseller’s catalog. I now run two. Tramaridge Press publishes the books under my own name, and The Fern publishes the novels under m kirk, so the two names stop bleeding into each other. Plus copyright. I registered it for CLUTCH. Balance went out before I knew to, so its paperwork is a tangle: the words are mine, but proving it on paper is something the lawyers will need to sort out before Anne Hathaway signs on to play Ellie in the movie. And there’s no Kindle edition of CLUTCH, on purpose: the book asks you to work in it with a pencil. That was a design choice, and it costs me readers every day. I’m OK with that; it was meant to be written in, and an ebook just doesn’t have that kind of vibe.

  • The Wrath of Archie Ellis gets everything the first two taught me. It’s a novel of Passchendaele, 1917, and it’s finished. The ISBN is mine, and this time it gets registered, and the publisher field checked, before I hit publish. I’m also building readers before launch, not after, which is Weir’s lesson. That starts with advance reader copies: free print copies for people willing to read early and post an honest review. On Instagram, I set up an automation: comment YPRES on my pinned post, or message me, and a reply arrives with the request form. Everything I post there also goes to a Facebook author page, and I joined a bunch of historical fiction and WW1 history groups. I have even (gasp) started a TikTok. I hold my nose every time I open it. The US company that now runs it still lists ByteDance as its largest single shareholder, and I’m not naive about where my data goes. But if it sells books, I’ll post.

Writing the books was the part I’d do for free. This is the rest of the job.

I think my novels are good. Not Great American Novel good, but better than some books I’ve read that came with film deals. I mean, they’re at least worth a Booker Short List, though. That matters less than I’d like. A good book nobody finds and a bad book nobody finds sell the same number of copies.

Talent is not a distribution strategy

I see the same pattern with the founders I coach. The best idea in the meeting doesn’t win. The idea with a path does: a sponsor, a forum, a route through the people who decide. Founders who say “the product speaks for itself” are usually the ones whose product nobody has heard of.

Quality is a precondition, not a plan. Weir had readers before he had a publisher. Scott had a name before she had a Substack. Whoever sold that debut novel had a pitch the rest of us never see. In every case, distribution came first, and the craft came along for the ride.

Luck is real. But luck needs somewhere to land. I’m building mine one comment trigger at a time, and this post is part of it.

Read it before anyone else does.

item.title: No job is finished until it leaves a note
item.dc:creator: Matt Goode
item.description: Systems don't break in the middle of the work. They break where it changes hands.
item.content:encoded:
Most work doesn’t get lost while someone is doing it. It gets lost in the gap between one person putting it down and the next person picking it up.

Hospitals learned this the expensive way. A patient’s care changes hands at every shift change, and for a long time that handoff was an informal verbal rundown. When nine pediatric residency programs replaced it with a structured routine called I-PASS, medical errors fell by 23 percent and preventable adverse events by 30 percent. Same doctors. Same patients. The only thing that changed was the handover.

That study stuck with me, because most of the founders I coach have the same problem. Most of them would also tell you they don’t do handovers at all.

You hand off to yourself all day

If you run a practice of one or a few, handovers can sound like a big-company problem. You don’t have shifts. There’s no one to hand to.

But you hand work over constantly. Morning You hands a proposal to Afternoon You. Monday You leaves a half-finished follow-up for Thursday You. The You Who Just Got Off a Client Call hands the next steps to the You Who Will Remember Them, eventually, probably.

Every one of those is a handover. Most of them happen in your head, with no note. That’s the hospital’s informal rundown, minus the hospital.

In my house this is a standing joke. I load the dishwasher, get distracted – squirrel – and forget to start it. I can’t tell you how many mornings I’ve come downstairs wanting coffee and found the French press still sitting in the dishwasher, dirty.

My wife never seems to have this problem. Or maybe she does, and I’ve forgotten, because she can remind me of things from years ago.

That’s a dropped handover. Evening Me did most of the job and handed the last step to nobody. Morning Me paid for it before coffee.

Here’s what the other kind looks like.

Those are book award deadlines for my next novel, WRATH, most of them months away. Fiction isn’t my main business, which is exactly why I would forget every one of them. So each task carries what future me will need: the hard deadline, a start date a week or so earlier, a reminder, and the small decision already made. Books must arrive by 12 February, not merely be posted by it. One copy from the November print order, trade cover only. October Me made those calls, so March Me doesn’t have to dig for them or get them wrong.

That’s a handover across six months, from me to me, and nobody had to remember anything.

You’ll also notice every task has a number. That’s the first of the three choices from my last essay: every task gets a permanent name. The word before the dash says which part of my work it belongs to. The number never changes and never gets reused, even if I rename the task. So a note can say “Done: WRATH-42,” and I can still find it a year from now. One task can point to another by its number. And when a list of questions is waiting on me, I can answer “WRATH-42 is fine, push WRATH-39” instead of explaining which awards thing I mean.

The note at the end of every job

When I built my own system, the rule I’m proudest of is the boring one. No job is finished until it leaves a note.

The note has three parts:

  1. What was done and decided. Two or three sentences, written as a story, not a status. Decisions matter more than activity, because you forget decisions first.

  2. What’s new. Any follow-up the job created goes onto the one shared list, with a name, before the job closes. Not buried in the note. On the list.

  3. What needs me, and what doesn’t. Anything waiting on a decision goes in a short numbered list, so I can answer by number. Everything else is already decided, and the note says so.

The next morning, the notes get read before anything else. That’s the last step in I-PASS, and it may matter most: the person taking over says back what they heard before the handover counts. A note nobody reads is just a diary. Nothing lives only in my head overnight.

The step leaders skip

DELEGATE, the framework in CLUTCH, has eight steps. The one leaders skip most is Transfer: the moment ownership actually changes hands.

Most delegation fails right there. The leader explains the work, sets the expectation, then hands it over in passing. The context stays in their head. Two weeks later, the work comes back wrong, and everyone concludes the person wasn’t ready.

Usually the person was fine. The handover wasn’t. You don’t have a delegation problem. You have a handover problem.

A good handover carries the same three things the note does: what’s already been decided, what’s still open, and what the new owner can decide without asking. That last one is the License. Leave it out, and the work boomerangs back to your desk, because the new owner can’t move without checking.

The same is true when the new owner is future you. If Thursday you doesn’t know what Monday you already decided, Thursday you will either redo the thinking or stall. Both feel like being busy. Neither is progress.

What changed

Here’s a small one. LinkedIn supposedly rewards you for posting the link to your essay a day later, in the comments, rather than with the post itself. I have never once remembered to do that. It’s too small a detail, and by the next day I’m onto something else. So I gave up and pasted the link in the comments as I posted, every time.

It isn’t even creative work. The comment is the same every time: “Click here for the full essay,” and the link. LinkedIn will let you schedule a post, but not a comment on it. So for now the comment gets its own task, with a name and a date, and when I miss it, the miss doesn’t vanish. It’s still on the list the next morning. I’m still working out how to automate the rest.

The surprise for me was that the note isn’t really for the system. It’s for the next person, and most days the next person is me.

Try it this week

You don’t need software for this. Take the next five things you finish this week, and before you call each one done, write three lines:

  1. What did I do, and what did I decide?

  2. What new tasks did this create, and where did I put them?

  3. What still needs a decision, and what can go ahead without one?

  4. If any of those take longer than a minute to answer, you’ve found where your work goes missing.

Where’s your leadership system breaking? →
